questions.problem:
The students in a particular school are split among three classes, class $1,$ class $2,$ and class $3.$

- Class $1$ contains $25%$ of the students in the school, and $55%$ of those students take biology.

- Class $2$ contains $35%$ of the students in the school, and $40%$ of those students take biology.

- Class $3$ contains $40%$ of the students in the school.

If $45%$ of students in the entire school are female, $80%$ of female students take biology, and $70%$ of biology students are female, what is the probability that a randomly selected student from class $3$ takes biology? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $F$ be the event that a student is female, $B$ be the event that a student takes biology, and ${C}_{1},{C}_{2},{C}_{3}$ be the event that a student is in class $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({C}_{1})=0.25 &  & P(B|{C}_{1})=0.55 \\  & P({C}_{2})=0.35 &  & P(B|{C}_{2})=0.4 \\  & P({C}_{3})=0.4\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${C}_{1}⊔{C}_{2}⊔{C}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({C}_{1})+P({C}_{2})+P({C}_{3})=0.25+0.35+0.4=1.
$$

- Since $45%$ of students in the entire school are female, we have

$$
P(F)=0.45.
$$

- Since $80%$ of females take biology, we have

$$
P(B|F)=0.8.
$$

- Since $70%$ of biology students are female, we have

$$
P(F|B)=0.7.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen student from class $3$ takes biology, which is represented as $P(B|{C}_{3}).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(F|B) & =\frac{P(B|F)P(F)}{P(B)} \\ P(F|B) & =\frac{P(B|F)P(F)}{P(B|{C}_{1})P({C}_{1})+P(B|{C}_{2})P({C}_{2})+P(B|{C}_{3})P({C}_{3})} \\ 0.7 & =\frac{(0.8)(0.45)}{(0.55)(0.25)+(0.4)(0.35)+P(B|{C}_{3})(0.4)} \\ 0.7 & =\frac{0.36}{0.2775+0.4P(B|{C}_{3})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(B|{C}_{3}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.7(0.2775+0.4P(B|{C}_{3})) & =0.36 \\ 0.2775+0.4P(B|{C}_{3}) & =\frac{0.36}{0.7} \\ 0.2775+0.4P(B|{C}_{3}) & =\frac{18}{35} \\ 0.4P(B|{C}_{3}) & =\frac{18}{35}-0.2775 \\ P(B|{C}_{3}) & =\frac{1}{0.4}(\frac{18}{35}-0.2775) \\ P(B|{C}_{3}) & ≈0.592\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

questions.problem:
A manufacturing company has three sites, factory $1,$ factory $2,$ and factory $3.$ They all produce two types of light bulbs: A and B.

- Factory $1$ produces $45%$ of the entire production, and $5%$ of those bulbs are defective.

- Factory $2$ produces $45%$ of the entire production.

- Factory $3$ produces $10%$ of the entire production, and $1%$ of those bulbs are defective.

If $57%$ of all light bulbs are of type A, $3%$ of type A light bulbs are defective, and $41%$ of defective light bulbs are of type A, what is the probability that a randomly chosen light bulb from factory $2$ is defective? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the event that a light bulb is of type A, $D$ be the event that a light bulb is defective, and ${F}_{1},{F}_{2},{F}_{3}$ be the event that a light bulb is produced in factory $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({F}_{1})=0.45 &  & P(D|{F}_{1})=0.05 \\  & P({F}_{2})=0.45 \\  & P({F}_{3})=0.1 &  & P(D|{F}_{3})=0.01\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${F}_{1}⊔{F}_{2}⊔{F}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({F}_{1})+P({F}_{2})+P({F}_{3})=0.45+0.45+0.1=1.
$$

- Since $57%$ of all light bulbs are of type A, we have

$$
P(A)=0.57.
$$

- Since $3%$ of type A light bulbs are defective, we have

$$
P(D|A)=0.03.
$$

- Since $41%$ of defective light bulbs are of type A, we have

$$
P(A|D)=0.41
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen light bulb from factory $2$ is defective, which is represented as $P(D|{F}_{2}).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A|D) & =\frac{P(D|A)P(A)}{P(D)} \\ P(A|D) & =\frac{P(D|A)P(A)}{P(D|{F}_{1})P({F}_{1})+P(D|{F}_{2})P({F}_{2})+P(D|{F}_{3})P({F}_{3})} \\ 0.41 & =\frac{(0.03)(0.57)}{(0.05)(0.45)+P(D|{F}_{2})(0.45)+(0.01)(0.1)} \\ 0.41 & =\frac{0.0171}{0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(D|{F}_{2}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.41(0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2})) & =0.0171 \\ 0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{0.0171}{0.41} \\ 0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{171}{4100} \\ 0.45P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{171}{4100}-0.0235 \\ P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{1}{0.45}(\frac{171}{4100}-0.0235) \\ P(D|{F}_{2}) & ≈0.040\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

questions.problem:
Arthur and Sara are finding the best recipe for chocolate muffins, and they test three different oven cooking modes, mode $1,$ mode $2,$ and mode $3.$ They also try two types of yeast, A and B.

- They use mode $1$ to cook the $30%$ of their muffins, and $90%$ of those muffins turn out well.

- They use mode $2$ to cook the $40%$ of their muffins, and $85%$ of those muffins turn out well.

- They use mode $3$ to cook the $30%$ of their muffins, and $88%$ of those muffins turn out well.

If $20%$ of all muffins was prepared with yeast A, and $87%$ of yeast A muffins turn out well, what is the probability that a randomly chosen good muffin is done with yeast A? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the event that a muffin is made with yeast A, $G$ be the event that a muffin turns out well, and ${M}_{1},{M}_{2},{M}_{3}$ be the event that a muffin is cooked with mode $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({M}_{1})=0.3 &  & P(G|{M}_{1})=0.9 \\  & P({M}_{2})=0.4 &  & P(G|{M}_{2})=0.85 \\  & P({M}_{3})=0.3 &  & P(G|{M}_{3})=0.88\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${M}_{1}⊔{M}_{2}⊔{M}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({M}_{1})+P({M}_{2})+P({M}_{3})=0.3+0.4+0.3=1.
$$

- Since $20%$ of muffins are made with yeast A, we have

$$
P(A)=0.2.
$$

- Since $87%$ of muffins made with yeast A turn out well, we have

$$
P(G|A)=0.87.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen good muffin is made with yeast A, which is represented as $P(A|G).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A|G) & =\frac{P(G|A)P(A)}{P(G)} \\  & =\frac{P(G|A)P(A)}{P(G|{M}_{1})P({M}_{1})+P(G|{M}_{2})P({M}_{2})+P(G|{M}_{3})P({M}_{3})} \\  & =\frac{(0.87)(0.2)}{(0.9)(0.3)+(0.85)(0.4)+(0.88)(0.3)} \\  & =\frac{0.174}{0.874} \\  & ≈0.199,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

questions.problem:
A volleyball school for children splits the players into three teams, team $1$, team $2,$ and team $3.$ 

- $44%$ of children are in team $1,$ and $23%$ of children in this team have been playing for over two years.

- $32%$ of children are in team $2,$ and $26%$ of children in this team have been playing for over two years.

- $24%$ of children are in team $3.$

If $7%$ of all children can play in the blocker position, $40%$ of children who can play as blockers have been playing for over two years, and $10%$ of children who have been playing for over two years can play as blockers, what is the probability that a randomly chosen child in team $3$ has been playing for over two years? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $B$ be the event that a child can play in the blocker position, $I$ be the event that a child has been playing for over two years, and ${T}_{1},{T}_{2},{T}_{3}$ be the events that a child is in team $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({T}_{1})=0.44 &  & P(I|{T}_{1})=0.23 \\  & P({T}_{2})=0.32 &  & P(I|{T}_{2})=0.26 \\  & P({T}_{3})=0.24\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${T}_{1}⊔{T}_{2}⊔{T}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({T}_{1})+P({T}_{2})+P({T}_{3})=0.44+0.32+0.24=1.
$$

- Since $7%$ of children can play in the blocker position, we have

$$
P(B)=0.07.
$$

- Since $40%$ of children who can play as blockers have been playing for over two years, we have

$$
P(I|B)=0.4.
$$

- Since $10%$ of children who have been playing for over two years can play as blockers, we have

$$
P(B|I)=0.1.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen child in team 3 has been playing for over two years, which is represented as $P(I|{T}_{3}).$

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(B|I) & =\frac{P(I|B)P(B)}{P(I)} \\ P(B|I) & =\frac{P(I|B)P(B)}{P(I|{T}_{1})P({T}_{1})+P(I|{T}_{2})P({T}_{2})+P(I|{T}_{3})P({T}_{3})} \\ 0.1 & =\frac{(0.4)(0.07)}{(0.23)(0.44)+(0.26)(0.32)+P(I|{T}_{3})(0.24)} \\ 0.1 & =\frac{0.028}{0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(I|{T}_{3}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.1(0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3})) & =0.028 \\ 0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{0.028}{0.1} \\ 0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{7}{25} \\ 0.24P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{7}{25}-0.1844 \\ P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{1}{0.24}(\frac{7}{25}-0.1844) \\ P(I|{T}_{3}) & ≈0.398\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

questions.problem:
In a nature park, there are $4$ species of squirrels, each with the same population.

- Among the squirrels of species $1,$ $12%$ are born in captivity.

- Among the squirrels of species $2,$ $5%$ are born in captivity.

- Among the squirrels of species $3,$ $6%$ are born in captivity.

- Among the squirrels of species $4,$ $3%$ are born in captivity.

If $35%$ of the squirrels are adult females, and $8%$ of the adult female squirrels are born in captivity, what is the probability that a randomly chosen squirrel born in captivity is an adult female? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $F$ be the event that a squirrel is an adult female, $C$ be the event that a squirrel is born in captivity, and ${S}_{1},{S}_{2},{S}_{3},{S}_{4}$ be the event that a squirrel is of species $1,$ $2,$ $3,$ or $4,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- Each species has the same number of squirrels, so we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned}P({S}_{1})=P({S}_{2})=P({S}_{3})=P({S}_{4})=0.25\end{aligned}
$$

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P(C|{S}_{1})=0.12 \\  & P(C|{S}_{2})=0.05 \\  & P(C|{S}_{3})=0.06 \\  & P(C|{S}_{4})=0.03\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${S}_{1}⊔{S}_{2}⊔{S}_{3}⊔{S}_{4}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({S}_{1})+P({S}_{2})+P({S}_{3})+P({S}_{4})=0.25+0.25+0.25+0.25=1.
$$

- Since $35%$ of the squirrels are adult females, we have

$$
P(F)=0.35.
$$

- Since $8%$ of adult females are born in captivity, we have

$$
P(C|F)=0.08.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen squirrel born in captivity is an adult female, which is represented as $P(F|C).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(F|C) & =\frac{P(C|F)P(F)}{P(C)} \\  & =\frac{P(C|F)P(F)}{P(C|{S}_{1})P({S}_{1})+P(C|{S}_{2})P({S}_{2})+P(C|{S}_{3})P({S}_{3})+P(C|{S}_{3})P({S}_{3})} \\  & =\frac{(0.08)(0.35)}{(0.12)(0.25)+(0.05)(0.25)+(0.06)(0.25)+(0.03)(0.25)} \\  & =\frac{0.028}{0.065} \\  & ≈0.431,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.
